questions.question: How do you configure Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for a Spring Boot service in Kubernetes?
questions.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for Spring Boot Services
questions.direct_answer: HPA adjusts replica count based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics. **Requires resource requests** on the container (the denominator in the utilization formula). For Spring Boot, CPU often misleads — I/O-bound services look idle while queued. Prefer custom metrics via Micrometer → Prometheus → Prometheus Adapter → HPA. Configure `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` (~300s) to prevent flapping. For event-driven workloads (Kafka, SQS), use KEDA instead — it can scale from zero.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Kubernetes autoscaling and its prerequisites (resource requests, metrics server, stabilization)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Omitting resource requests (HPA reports `<unknown>` and never scales), or scaling CPU for an I/O-bound service that never shows CPU load
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the metrics pipeline (Metrics Server vs Prometheus Adapter), scale-down stabilization, PDB interaction with scale-down, KEDA for event-driven, and HPA + Cluster Autoscaler coupling

sections.title: Why CPU-Based Scaling Misleads You About Spring Boot Traffic Load
sections.content:
HPA's default metric — CPU utilization — works well for CPU-bound workloads like image processing. For a typical Spring Boot REST service, **CPU tells you almost nothing about actual load**. A service handling 500 requests per second may sit at 20% CPU because most of the latency is I/O wait on database calls. HPA sees low CPU, keeps the replica count low, and the service drowns in queued requests while CPU looks idle.

The formula: **HPA calculates utilization as `current / request`**. If you request 250m CPU and the pod uses 175m, HPA sees 70% — regardless of whether the pod is handling 10 requests or 10,000. Without resource requests defined at all, HPA has no denominator and cannot function — the target shows `<unknown>` and pods never scale.

**Custom metrics** — requests per second, latency percentile, queue depth — give HPA semantically meaningful inputs. Instead of "is this pod using a lot of CPU?" you ask "is this pod handling more requests than it should?" The pipeline: Spring Boot Micrometer → Prometheus scrapes → Prometheus Adapter exposes custom metrics API → HPA queries.

sections.title: The Autoscaling Metrics Pipeline
sections.content:
HPA polls the metrics APIs every 15s (configurable). Metrics Server handles CPU/memory; Prometheus Adapter handles custom metrics. A separate layer (Cluster Autoscaler) adds nodes when pods cannot schedule.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    App[Spring Boot pod\n/actuator/prometheus] --> MS[Metrics Server\nCPU, memory]
    App --> Prom[Prometheus\nscrapes Micrometer]
    Prom --> PA[Prometheus Adapter]
    MS -->|metrics.k8s.io| HPA
    PA -->|custom.metrics.k8s.io| HPA[HorizontalPodAutoscaler]
    HPA -->|replicas desired| Deploy[Deployment]
    Deploy --> Pods[Pods]
    Pods --> SchedulerCheck{Can pod schedule?}
    SchedulerCheck -->|No, Pending| CA[Cluster Autoscaler\n/ Karpenter]
    CA -->|add node| Nodes[Node pool]
    Nodes --> Pods
```

HPA and Cluster Autoscaler are coupled in production: HPA scales pods, Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes when pods cannot fit. Without the autoscaler, HPA can request replicas that stay `Pending` forever.

sections.title: The Prerequisite Everyone Forgets: Resource Requests Are the Denominator
sections.content:
HPA's CPU formula is `current CPU usage / CPU request * 100`. Without a CPU request, this has no denominator and HPA reports `<unknown>` — pods never scale even under massive load.

The target utilization (typically 70%) determines the threshold: `desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas * currentUtilization / targetUtilization)`. If 3 pods average 90% CPU with 70% target, HPA computes `ceil(3 * 90/70) = 4` and scales up.

**`minReplicas` and `maxReplicas`** bound the range. Always set `minReplicas >= 2` for availability — a single pod during scale-down means a restart takes the service offline. Set `maxReplicas` to cap runaway scaling from feedback loops.

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: spring-app-hpa}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: spring-app
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70}
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: memory
        target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80}
```

Multiple metrics — HPA computes desired replicas for each and picks the **maximum**. This prevents undersizing during bursts that dominate only one dimension.

sections.title: Custom Metrics From Micrometer Give You Meaningful Scaling Triggers
Stabilization Windows Prevent Scale-Down Flapping
sections.content:
Without stabilization, HPA reacts to momentary metric changes. A brief traffic dip → scale down → traffic returns → scale up. Each scale-down terminates pods, losing warm JVM caches and connection pools. Each scale-up starts cold pods that take 30+ seconds to serve traffic. This **flapping** wastes resources and degrades latency.

`behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` requires the metric to stay below threshold for a sustained period before removing replicas.

```yaml
behavior:
  scaleUp:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
    policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 100       # double the replicas
        periodSeconds: 15
      - type: Pods
        value: 4         # or add 4 pods
        periodSeconds: 15
    selectPolicy: Max    # use whichever adds more
  scaleDown:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300   # 5 min sustained low before scaling down
    policies:
      - type: Pods
        value: 1
        periodSeconds: 60   # at most 1 pod/min
```

**Asymmetric behavior:** aggressive scale-up (double every 15s), conservative scale-down (remove 1 pod/min after 5 min stable). Matches the cost profile — adding capacity is cheap, removing prematurely costs warm cache and startup latency.

**PodDisruptionBudget + HPA interaction.** A PDB with `minAvailable: 2` limits voluntary disruptions including HPA scale-down evictions. If HPA tries to scale from 2 to 1 but PDB says minimum 2, the eviction is blocked. Tune PDB and HPA `minReplicas` to be consistent.

sections.title: HPA Pitfalls, When to Reach for KEDA or VPA, and Graceful Shutdown
sections.content:
**Common HPA pitfalls:**

- **Missing resource requests** — HPA shows `<unknown>`. First diagnostic: `kubectl describe hpa` shows the target unreachable.
- **Wrong metric for the workload** — CPU on an I/O-bound service never triggers; switch to RPS or latency-based custom metrics.
- **`minReplicas: 1`** — single-pod windows risk outages during scale events; always `minReplicas >= 2` for production.
- **No Cluster Autoscaler** — HPA requests more pods, scheduler cannot fit, pods stay Pending, incident on the dashboard.
- **No graceful shutdown** — HPA scales down → kubelet SIGTERM — Spring Boot must handle `server.shutdown=graceful` with `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s` and a `preStop` hook that sleeps briefly so LB has time to drain.

**When HPA is not enough:**

- **KEDA** for event-driven workloads: Kafka consumer lag, SQS depth, RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, Prometheus expressions. Scales from 0 to N; HPA cannot.
- **VPA** for right-sizing: observes actual usage and recommends or auto-adjusts requests/limits. Run in `recommend` mode first.
- **Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter** for node capacity: no point scaling pods if nodes cannot fit them.

**Don't run HPA and VPA together on the same Deployment for CPU/memory** — they fight (HPA scales replicas based on utilization, VPA resizes the pod changing what utilization means). VPA can coexist with HPA if HPA uses custom metrics and VPA only manages memory, not CPU.

**Observability the HPA needs:**
- Prometheus metric `kube_hpa_status_current_replicas` vs `kube_hpa_spec_max_replicas` — alert at 80% of max (approaching runaway or capacity).
- `kube_hpa_status_condition{condition="ScalingLimited"}` — HPA wanted more but hit `maxReplicas`.
- Application readiness latency during cold starts — if scale-up is not keeping up with traffic, increase `scaleUp` aggressiveness.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Resource requests are HPA's denominator** — without CPU requests HPA reports `<unknown>` and never scales; the #1 misconfiguration.
- **CPU utilization misleads I/O-bound services** — use custom metrics (RPS, latency, queue depth) via Prometheus Adapter for semantically meaningful triggers.
- **Scale-down stabilization prevents flapping** — `stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300` requires 5 min of sustained low before removing pods.
- **Asymmetric scale behavior** — aggressive up, conservative down; matches cost profile where added capacity is cheap but losing warm caches is expensive.
- **HPA + Cluster Autoscaler are coupled** — HPA scales pods, CA scales nodes; without CA, HPA-requested pods stay Pending.
- **KEDA scales from zero for event-driven** — Kafka lag, SQS depth, queue-based; HPA cannot because `minReplicas >= 1`.
- **Do not combine HPA and VPA on CPU/memory** — they fight; use HPA with custom metrics and VPA on a different dimension or not at all.
- **Graceful shutdown is required** — Spring `server.shutdown=graceful` + `preStop` hook + LB drain; without it scale-down drops in-flight requests.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler watches a metric and adjusts the replica count to keep it near a target. For Spring Boot APIs, CPU utilization is the standard starting point — when CPU climbs above target, HPA adds replicas; when it drops, HPA removes them.

**How HPA calculates scaling**
- Divides current metric by target: target CPU 50%, actual 80% → factor 1.6 → 3 replicas become 5.
- Requires metrics-server for CPU/memory — `kubectl top pods` working confirms the pipeline; HPA showing `<unknown>` means the metrics server is missing or requests are undefined.
- Respects minReplicas and maxReplicas as hard bounds; set minReplicas high enough to handle sudden spikes before autoscaling reacts.

**Scale-down cooldown**
- Scales up aggressively (within 15 seconds) but conservatively down; default 5-minute stabilization before further reduction prevents flapping under variable load.
- Adjust `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` — shorter for stateless services that restart cheaply; longer for services with slow warm-up.
- Scale-down marks the count on the Deployment but actual termination follows `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` — ensure Spring Boot's graceful shutdown is configured so in-flight requests complete.

**Custom metrics**
- Via Micrometer → Prometheus → Prometheus Adapter → custom.metrics.k8s.io; HPA targets RPS or p95 latency or queue depth — semantically meaningful for business load.
- A Kafka consumer with 10,000 messages lag needs more replicas even at 5% CPU; CPU HPA never triggers — use KEDA which scales on Kafka lag directly and can scale from zero, which HPA cannot.

**Production gotchas**
- Pair HPA with Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter — without node-level scaling, HPA-requested pods stay Pending when nodes are full.
- Don't run HPA and VPA together on the same CPU/memory dimension — they fight and cause oscillation.
- Alert on `kube_hpa_status_condition{condition="ScalingLimited"}` — means you hit maxReplicas and traffic is not being absorbed.

questions.question: How does KEDA enable event-driven autoscaling and when should you use it instead of HPA?
questions.title: KEDA: Event-Driven Autoscaling for Kafka Consumers and Queue Workers
questions.direct_answer: KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaler) scales workloads based on external event sources — Kafka consumer lag, SQS queue depth, RabbitMQ messages, Prometheus queries, CRON expressions, Redis streams, and 60+ built-in scalers. It can scale **from zero to N and back to zero** when idle — something HPA cannot do because HPA requires `minReplicas >= 1`. KEDA internally creates an HPA under the hood for the scaling-from-1-to-N range, plus its own controller for 0↔1. Use KEDA for consumers and batch workers; keep HPA for request-driven services.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how to autoscale consumers/workers where HPA is insufficient
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using HPA CPU scaling on a Kafka consumer (consumer is I/O-bound, CPU never triggers, lag climbs, SLA breaches) or running idle workers 24/7 because HPA can't scale to zero
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the ScaledObject vs ScaledJob distinction, cooldown period, polling interval tuning, how KEDA creates an HPA internally, composition with Istio/Knative, and cost savings from scale-to-zero

sections.title: Why HPA Fails for Kafka Consumers and Queue Workers
sections.content:
A Kafka consumer is processing orders. Traffic doubles — consumer lag grows from 1,000 to 100,000 messages. The consumer pod's CPU is 15% because most time is spent waiting on poll calls and downstream DB writes. HPA's CPU-based scaling sees 15% — far below the 70% threshold — and **does nothing**. Lag keeps climbing. SLA breaks.

The root cause: **HPA scales on resource utilization, not work backlog**. For request-driven services, CPU + request count correlate with load. For event-driven consumers and workers, they do not. The right signal is the **queue depth or consumer lag**, which lives outside Kubernetes.

**KEDA solves this** by making external event sources first-class scaling metrics. Install KEDA in the cluster, declare a `ScaledObject` pointing at a Kafka topic with a lag threshold, and the consumer scales based on lag — not CPU. KEDA supports **60+ event sources** (Kafka, AWS SQS, RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, Google Pub/Sub, NATS, Redis streams, Prometheus metrics, CRON, HTTP rate via Prometheus).

**The second HPA limitation KEDA solves: scale to zero.** HPA requires `minReplicas >= 1` — you pay for one replica always. For periodic batch workers or low-volume consumers, this wastes money. KEDA scales **from zero to N and back to zero** when idle, commonly a 40–80% cost reduction for bursty workloads.

sections.title: KEDA Architecture: Agent, Metrics Adapter, and the Embedded HPA
sections.content:
KEDA is not a replacement for HPA — it composes with HPA. KEDA owns the 0↔1 transition; HPA handles 1→N.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Cluster
        Agent[KEDA Operator\ncontrols 0<->1]
        Adapter[KEDA Metrics Adapter\nexposes external metrics API]
        HPA[Auto-generated HPA\nscales 1..N]
        SO[ScaledObject CRD\nrefs Deployment + trigger]
        Deploy[Deployment\nKafka consumer]
    end
    subgraph External[External event sources]
        Kafka[Kafka topic lag]
        SQS[AWS SQS queue depth]
        Prom[Prometheus query]
    end
    Kafka -.poll lag.-> Agent
    SQS -.poll depth.-> Agent
    Prom -.query.-> Agent
    SO --> Agent
    Agent -->|activate: scale 0->1| Deploy
    Agent -->|create| HPA
    HPA --> Adapter
    Adapter -->|external.metrics.k8s.io| HPA
    HPA -->|scale 1..N replicas| Deploy
```

The flow: Operator polls event source. If lag > activation threshold, scale Deployment from 0 to 1. For further scaling, HPA consumes metrics from KEDA's Metrics Adapter and scales 1→N. When idle for `cooldownPeriod`, Operator scales back to 0.

sections.title: Installing KEDA and Defining a Kafka ScaledObject
sections.content:
**Install:** Helm chart in the `keda` namespace. No app code change. After install, three components run: `keda-operator`, `keda-metrics-apiserver`, `keda-admission-webhooks`.

```bash
helm install keda kedacore/keda --namespace keda --create-namespace
kubectl get pods -n keda
```

**Define a ScaledObject** for a Kafka consumer Deployment. The consumer already exists as a plain Deployment — KEDA wraps it.

```yaml
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: order-consumer
  namespace: prod
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: order-consumer         # Deployment name
  minReplicaCount: 0             # scale to ZERO when idle
  maxReplicaCount: 20
  pollingInterval: 15            # check lag every 15s
  cooldownPeriod: 300            # 5 min of no activity -> scale to 0
  triggers:
    - type: kafka
      metadata:
        bootstrapServers: kafka.kafka:9092
        consumerGroup: order-consumer-group
        topic: orders
        lagThreshold: "1000"       # 1 replica per 1000 msg lag
        activationLagThreshold: "50"  # wake up from 0 when lag > 50
```

**Behavior:**
- Lag 0, pod count 0 — KEDA polls Kafka every 15s.
- Lag hits 60 — above `activationLagThreshold` — KEDA scales deployment 0→1.
- Lag hits 5,000 — HPA (auto-created) scales 1→5 replicas (5,000 / 1,000).
- Lag drops to 0 — after 300s cooldown, KEDA scales to 0.

**Authentication:** `TriggerAuthentication` CRD pulls credentials from Secrets, Vault, or cloud IAM — KEDA does not embed secrets in ScaledObjects.

sections.title: ScaledObject vs ScaledJob: Long-Running vs Per-Message
sections.content:
KEDA has two workload types with different semantics.

**`ScaledObject`** scales a Deployment (or StatefulSet). The workload is **long-running** — one replica can process many messages over its lifetime. Right choice for Kafka consumers that hold connection and consumer-group membership, or HTTP API workers.

**`ScaledJob`** creates a Job per queue event. The workload is **per-message** — one Job per message, completes and exits. Right choice for batch image processing, one-off ETL tasks, or anything where each message triggers isolated work.

```yaml
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledJob
metadata: {name: image-processor}
spec:
  jobTargetRef:
    template:
      spec:
        containers:
          - name: processor
            image: my-image-processor:1.0
        restartPolicy: OnFailure
  maxReplicaCount: 50
  triggers:
    - type: aws-sqs-queue
      metadata:
        queueURL: https://sqs.../image-queue
        queueLength: "5"    # 1 Job per 5 messages
        awsRegion: us-east-1
```

Each batch of 5 messages triggers a new Job pod; pod exits after processing; up to 50 concurrent.

**Rule of thumb:** consumer groups, HTTP workers → `ScaledObject`. Per-event batch processing, ML inference, image rendering → `ScaledJob`.

sections.title: KEDA vs HPA, Scale-to-Zero Considerations, and Production Gotchas
sections.content:
**KEDA vs HPA decision matrix:**

| Signal | Choice |
|---|---|
| CPU/memory | HPA |
| HTTP RPS (via Prometheus) | HPA with custom metrics OR KEDA with Prometheus scaler |
| Kafka consumer lag | KEDA |
| SQS / RabbitMQ / Azure Service Bus | KEDA |
| Scheduled (CRON) scaling | KEDA |
| Idle workloads needing scale-to-zero | KEDA |
| Per-message isolated work | KEDA ScaledJob |

**Scale-to-zero considerations:**

- **Cold start latency.** First message waits for pod creation + container pull + JVM warmup — 30–60s for Spring Boot. For latency-sensitive flows, keep `minReplicaCount: 1`.
- **Polling cost.** `pollingInterval: 15` means KEDA polls Kafka every 15s even when idle. Usually negligible; for very large scaler counts, raise interval.
- **Cooldown tuning.** Too short → flapping 0↔1→0 during bursty traffic. Too long → you pay for idle pods. Start at 300s, adjust.
- **Activation vs scaling threshold.** `activationLagThreshold` is the wake-up signal from 0; `lagThreshold` is the per-replica target. Setting activation too low wakes up too eagerly; too high delays start-up during genuine load.

**Production gotchas:**

- **Kafka consumer groups need rebalancing time** — rapid scale events cause repeated rebalance storms; ensure the group's `session.timeout.ms` is tuned and the consumer handles rebalance gracefully.
- **Graceful shutdown on scale-down** — KEDA sends SIGTERM; the consumer must finish processing in-flight messages before exiting. Spring Kafka: set `kafka.listener.idleBetweenPolls` + listener `stop()` on shutdown.
- **Rate limits on cloud scalers** — KEDA polls AWS SQS / Azure Service Bus APIs; at many ScaledObjects + short polling intervals, you can hit cloud API rate limits. Use shared `TriggerAuthentication` and reasonable polling.
- **PDB + scale-to-zero conflict** — a PDB with `minAvailable: 1` prevents scale-to-zero; use `maxUnavailable` instead.
- **HPA generated by KEDA is managed** — do not edit it directly; edit the ScaledObject and KEDA regenerates.

**Cost observation.** For bursty consumer workloads (batch ingestion, nightly ETL), scale-to-zero typically saves 40–80% of compute vs keeping `minReplicas: 1` 24/7. Measure with `container_memory_usage_bytes * hours-running` before and after adoption.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **KEDA scales on external event signals** — Kafka lag, SQS depth, RabbitMQ, Prometheus, CRON, 60+ scalers; HPA cannot scale on signals outside Kubernetes.
- **KEDA scales from zero** — HPA requires `minReplicas >= 1`; KEDA owns the 0↔1 transition; combined with HPA it scales 1→N internally.
- **`ScaledObject` for long-running, `ScaledJob` for per-message** — Kafka consumers and HTTP workers use ScaledObject; per-event batch work uses ScaledJob (one Job per batch).
- **Cold start is the main scale-to-zero cost** — 30–60s JVM warmup; for latency-sensitive paths keep `minReplicaCount: 1`.
- **Activation threshold vs scaling threshold** — activation wakes from 0; scaling threshold is per-replica target for ongoing; tune separately.
- **Cooldown period prevents flapping** — start at 300s; balance idle cost vs rapid re-scale-up latency.
- **Graceful shutdown still matters** — consumers must handle SIGTERM cleanly so in-flight messages are committed, not lost or double-processed.
- **KEDA generates an HPA; do not edit it** — edit the ScaledObject; KEDA reconciles.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
KEDA is Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling — it scales workloads based on external event sources like Kafka consumer lag, SQS queue depth, RabbitMQ messages, or Prometheus queries. It composes with HPA rather than replacing it.

**Why it exists**
- HPA requires resource utilization to be the scaling signal and a minimum of 1 replica always running.
- A Kafka consumer at 15% CPU with lag climbing to 100,000 messages is exactly the scenario HPA cannot handle — CPU never crosses threshold, lag keeps growing.
- KEDA makes queue depth and consumer lag first-class scaling metrics, and scales from zero for idle workloads.

**Architecture**
- KEDA runs three components: operator, metrics adapter, admission webhooks.
- A ScaledObject CRD points at a Deployment and declares triggers — Kafka lag, SQS depth, whatever.
- KEDA owns the 0↔1 transition — when activation threshold is crossed, it scales the Deployment from zero to one.
- For 1→N scaling, KEDA auto-generates an HPA that reads metrics from KEDA's metrics adapter; developers don't touch this HPA, edits happen on the ScaledObject.

**ScaledObject vs ScaledJob**
- ScaledObject wraps a long-running Deployment — right choice for Kafka consumers, HTTP workers, anything that runs continuously and handles many messages per replica.
- ScaledJob creates a Job per event batch — right for per-message isolated work like ML inference, image processing, one-off ETL; each message spawns a fresh pod that exits when done.

**Scale-to-zero considerations**
- Cold start latency is the main cost — 30 to 60 seconds for a Spring Boot JVM; for latency-critical paths keep minReplicaCount at 1.
- Cooldown period controls flapping — 5 minutes of idle before scaling back to zero is a good default.
- For bursty workloads like nightly ETL or batch ingestion, scale-to-zero saves 40 to 80 percent on compute vs leaving one replica running 24/7.

**Production gotchas**
- Kafka consumer groups rebalance on every scale event — tune session.timeout.ms and handle rebalance listener events gracefully.
- Graceful shutdown is mandatory — KEDA sends SIGTERM, the consumer must commit in-flight messages before exiting or messages are re-processed on the next scale-up.
- PDB with minAvailable blocks scale-to-zero — use maxUnavailable instead for PDB on KEDA-managed Deployments.
- Don't edit the auto-generated HPA; it is owned by KEDA and reconciles on every change; edit the ScaledObject instead.

beats.text: A Kafka consumer is processing orders. Traffic doubles — consumer lag grows from 1,000 to 100,000 messages. The consumer pod's CPU is 15% because most time is spent waiting on poll calls and downstream DB writes. HPA's CPU-based scaling sees 15% — far below the 70% threshold — and does nothing. Lag keeps climbing. SLA breaks. The root cause: HPA scales on resource utilization, not work backlog. For request-driven services, CPU + request count correlate with load. For event-driven consumers and workers, they do not. The right signal is the queue depth or consumer lag, which lives outside Kubernetes. KEDA solves this by making external event sources first-class scaling metrics. Install KEDA in the cluster, declare a ScaledObject pointing at.

items: Using HPA CPU scaling on a Kafka consumer (consumer is I/O-bound, CPU never triggers, lag climbs, SLA breaches) or running idle workers 24/7 because HPA can't scale to zero

questions.question: How does Cluster Autoscaler work and how does Karpenter improve on it?
questions.title: Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter: Node-Level Scaling in Kubernetes
questions.direct_answer: **Cluster Autoscaler (CA)** adds nodes when pods are Pending and removes nodes that are underutilized. It operates on pre-defined **node groups** (ASGs) and has coarse scaling granularity — you get whatever instance type the group is. **Karpenter** (AWS, with Azure support) is node-group-less: it looks at the exact CPU/memory of pending pods, picks the cheapest EC2 instance type that fits (including Spot and mixed instance types), and provisions in 30–60s vs CA's 3–5 min. Karpenter is faster, cheaper, and more flexible — now the default choice for new EKS clusters. GKE has its own autoscaler with similar capabilities.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of node-level scaling, not just pod-level; and whether you've followed the Karpenter evolution
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking HPA alone provides elasticity (no, it scales pods but if nodes are full, pods stay Pending); or ignoring Spot instances for cost
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the pod-level signal both autoscalers use (Pending pods), how Karpenter bypasses ASGs, Spot interruption handling (Karpenter's node drain on rebalance recommendation), cost savings from right-sized instances, and how HPA/KEDA + Karpenter compose

sections.title: The Missing Piece: HPA Scales Pods, But Nodes Don't Grow Themselves
sections.content:
You configured HPA to scale replicas from 3 to 30 under load. Traffic spikes, HPA requests 30 replicas, and 27 of them sit in `Pending` with `FailedScheduling: Insufficient cpu`. Your app has elasticity in theory; in practice you ran out of node capacity.

**HPA scales pods. A separate component scales nodes.** Two main choices:

- **Cluster Autoscaler (CA)** — open-source, works on all clouds (AWS, GCP, Azure, on-prem). Operates on pre-defined node groups (ASGs in AWS, MIGs in GCP). When a pod is Pending and would fit on a new node in some group, CA scales that group up. When a node is underutilized and its pods could move to other nodes, CA drains and terminates it.
- **Karpenter** — open-source, originally AWS-only, now supports Azure. **Node-group-less**: looks at pending pods' exact resource shape and picks the cheapest matching instance type from the cloud catalog (including Spot). Provisions 5–10x faster than CA (30–60s vs 3–5 min). Becoming the default for new EKS clusters.
- **Cloud-native autoscalers** (GKE Autopilot, EKS Auto Mode) — fully managed; you don't see nodes at all.

**Together with HPA/KEDA**, the autoscaler completes the elasticity story: HPA/KEDA sizes the pod count, Karpenter/CA sizes the node pool.

sections.title: Two Models: Node-Group-Driven (CA) vs Pod-Shape-Driven (Karpenter)
sections.content:
Both react to `Pending` pods but decide differently about what to provision.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph CAModel[Cluster Autoscaler \(traditional\)]
        HPA1[HPA scales pods] --> PodA[Pending pod\nrequests 2 CPU, 4Gi]
        PodA --> CA[Cluster Autoscaler]
        CA -->|pick matching group| NG1[Node Group A\nm5.large]
        CA -->|or| NG2[Node Group B\nc5.xlarge]
        NG1 -->|ASG scale +1| Node1[New node m5.large\n3 min boot]
    end
    subgraph KarpenterModel[Karpenter]
        HPA2[HPA scales pods] --> PodB[Pending pod\nrequests 2 CPU, 4Gi]
        PodB --> K[Karpenter Controller]
        K -->|bin-pack + cost| EC2API[EC2 API\nFleet create]
        EC2API -->|pick cheapest fit\nm5.large Spot| Node2[New node\n30-60s boot]
    end
```

CA picks from pre-defined groups. Karpenter picks from the entire cloud catalog per pending pod, optimizing for cost and fit. Result: Karpenter often runs 30–50% cheaper for variable workloads.

sections.title: Cluster Autoscaler: How It Works and Where It Hurts
sections.content:
CA runs as a Deployment in `kube-system`. It watches:

- **Pending pods** with `reason: Unschedulable` due to insufficient resources.
- **Node utilization** — nodes using <50% of requests are candidates for removal.

**Scale-up flow:**

1. Pod Pending → CA simulates scheduling on each configured node group — would a new node in this group fit the pod?
2. Pick the best-matching group (based on cost hints, labels).
3. Increase the group's desired size via cloud API (ASG, MIG).
4. Cloud boots node (3–5 min: EC2 start + AMI + kubelet join).
5. Kubelet joins, scheduler places the pod.

**Scale-down flow:**

1. Node underutilized for 10 minutes (tunable).
2. CA drains (respecting PDBs) — evicts pods one at a time.
3. Terminates node once drained.

**Example config (AWS):**

```yaml
# values.yaml for cluster-autoscaler helm chart
autoDiscovery:
  clusterName: my-cluster
extraArgs:
  scale-down-utilization-threshold: 0.5
  scale-down-unneeded-time: 10m
  balance-similar-node-groups: true
  expander: least-waste
awsRegion: us-east-1
```

**Pain points:**

- **Node group complexity.** You must pre-define groups for every instance type / zone combo; variable workloads need many groups.
- **Slow scale-up.** 3–5 min for a new node; Pending pods back up during the wait.
- **No bin-packing across instance types.** If pending pod needs 4 CPU and only an m5.large (2 CPU) group is available, CA cannot pick a larger type from another pre-defined group automatically.
- **Spot handling is per-group.** Mixed Spot/On-Demand requires separate groups; CA cannot dynamically rebalance.

sections.title: Karpenter: Node-Group-Less, Fast, and Cost-Aware
sections.content:
Karpenter is **provisioner-based, not group-based**. A `NodePool` (v1) says "provision any instance from this list of families, zones, and architectures; honor these constraints." Karpenter picks a specific instance per pending pod shape.

```yaml
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata: {name: default}
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category
          operator: In
          values: ["c", "m", "r"]
        - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-generation
          operator: Gt
          values: ["2"]
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["spot", "on-demand"]
        - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          operator: In
          values: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]
      nodeClassRef:
        name: default
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 30s
```

**Scale-up flow:**

1. Pod Pending.
2. Karpenter bin-packs pending pods into a synthetic node shape.
3. Queries EC2 API for instance types matching the NodePool's requirements + fitting the shape.
4. Picks cheapest (Spot preferred when available); launches via EC2 Fleet.
5. Node boots (30–60s) and joins cluster.

**Consolidation (scale-down):** Karpenter continuously evaluates whether the current fleet can be replaced with fewer / smaller / cheaper nodes. Drains and replaces nodes to save money. This is where real cost wins come from — Karpenter right-sizes the fleet every minute.

**Spot interruption handling:** Karpenter subscribes to EC2 interruption events and rebalance recommendations. Gets 2-minute warning, cordons the node, initiates drain, provisions replacement — all before AWS reclaims the instance.

**Why it's faster than CA:**

- No pre-defined groups to search through.
- Direct EC2 Fleet API call, not ASG scale-up.
- Boots a raw instance rather than waiting for an ASG to launch-template-instantiate.

sections.title: Choosing, Tuning, and Composition With HPA/KEDA
sections.content:
**Karpenter vs Cluster Autoscaler:**

| | Cluster Autoscaler | Karpenter |
|---|---|---|
| Clouds | All (AWS, GCP, Azure, on-prem) | AWS, Azure (OSS) |
| Node groups | Required, pre-defined | None; per-pod decision |
| Scale-up speed | 3–5 min | 30–60s |
| Instance flexibility | Limited to group's types | Full cloud catalog |
| Spot support | Per-group | First-class, mixed |
| Consolidation | Basic utilization check | Continuous re-bin-packing |
| Cost savings | Baseline | 20–50% lower for variable workloads |

**When to pick Cluster Autoscaler:**

- Multi-cloud or on-prem.
- Existing ASG/MIG infrastructure and tooling.
- Stable workloads where node-group simplicity matters more than cost optimization.

**When to pick Karpenter:**

- AWS-heavy, variable or bursty workloads.
- Want aggressive cost optimization via Spot + right-sizing.
- Growing service count where pre-defining node groups becomes painful.

**Composition with HPA/KEDA:**

- HPA scales Deployment replicas → replicas become pods → pods Pending → autoscaler provisions node.
- KEDA scales from 0 on queue depth → first pod Pending → autoscaler provisions node.
- **Karpenter's 30–60s scale-up + KEDA's scale-from-zero** produces the fastest end-to-end response to bursts in a queue.

**Production gotchas:**

- **PodDisruptionBudgets** — both autoscalers honor PDBs during consolidation; without PDBs, consolidation may disrupt availability.
- **Node-local state** — DaemonSets, local PVs; consolidation churns nodes, DaemonSets re-init cost is real at scale.
- **Graceful termination** — consolidation drains nodes; apps need working graceful shutdown.
- **Multi-AZ Spot** — same instance type across 3 AZs reduces simultaneous interruption risk.
- **Limits on pod density** — AWS VPC CNI has IP/ENI limits per instance type; small instances (t3.small) run only ~10 pods. Karpenter's bin-packing must respect this.
- **Karpenter consolidation can be aggressive** — `consolidateAfter: 30s` moves pods frequently; use `WhenEmpty` (only drain empty nodes) for more stability, `WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized` for max savings.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HPA scales pods; Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter scales nodes** — without node autoscaling, HPA-requested pods stay Pending; both layers together give real elasticity.
- **Cluster Autoscaler needs pre-defined node groups** — scales ASGs based on Pending pods; 3–5 min provisioning; limited instance flexibility per group.
- **Karpenter is node-group-less** — picks cheapest matching instance from the full cloud catalog per pending pod; 30–60s boot; continuous consolidation.
- **Karpenter saves 20–50% on variable workloads** — bin-packing, Spot-first, right-sizing; measurable on EKS compute bills after adoption.
- **Consolidation continuously re-bin-packs** — Karpenter evaluates whether the fleet can be replaced with fewer/cheaper nodes every minute; drains respecting PDBs.
- **Spot interruption handled gracefully** — Karpenter subscribes to EC2 rebalance events, cordons, drains, and provisions replacement before reclaim.
- **Compose with HPA + KEDA** — HPA/KEDA for pod count, Karpenter for node capacity; fastest end-to-end response to bursts.
- **PDBs + graceful shutdown are mandatory** — both autoscalers drain nodes; without PDBs and working graceful shutdown, consolidation causes availability hits.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HPA scales pods, but pods need nodes to run on. When HPA requests 30 replicas and the cluster has room for 3, 27 pods stay Pending. Node-level autoscaling is the other half of the elasticity story.

**Cluster Autoscaler**
- Open source, works on all clouds, operates on pre-defined node groups (ASGs on AWS, MIGs on GCP).
- Watches Pending pods; when a pod cannot schedule on any existing node, CA picks a matching node group and tells the cloud to scale that ASG up.
- Scale-up takes 3 to 5 minutes — EC2 boot + AMI + kubelet join; Pending pods back up during the wait.
- Scale-down drains under-utilized nodes (below 50% requests for 10 minutes by default) respecting PodDisruptionBudgets.

**Karpenter**
- Open source, originally AWS, now Azure too; replaces Cluster Autoscaler for those clouds.
- Node-group-less — looks at the exact resource shape of pending pods and queries the EC2 catalog for the cheapest instance type that fits; provisions via EC2 Fleet API.
- Scale-up is 30 to 60 seconds vs CA's 3 to 5 minutes — 5 to 10 times faster because there is no ASG indirection.
- Consolidation continuously re-evaluates whether the fleet can be replaced with fewer or cheaper nodes; drains and replaces respecting PDBs.
- First-class Spot support with mixed Spot/on-demand in one NodePool; subscribes to EC2 interruption events so it can drain and provision replacement before AWS reclaims the instance.

**Cost impact**
- On variable workloads, Karpenter typically runs 20 to 50 percent cheaper than Cluster Autoscaler because it picks right-sized instances and leverages Spot aggressively.
- For stable workloads the savings are smaller but still positive due to continuous consolidation removing idle capacity.

**How they compose with HPA and KEDA**
- HPA or KEDA scales the Deployment replica count — replicas become Pods — Pods Pending — the cluster autoscaler adds a node.
- With KEDA scaling from zero and Karpenter provisioning nodes in under a minute, end-to-end wake-up from zero to serving a burst is measurable in one to two minutes.

**When to pick each**
- Karpenter on AWS or Azure with variable workloads and cost optimization pressure — the default recommendation now for new EKS clusters.
- Cluster Autoscaler for multi-cloud, on-prem, or stable workloads where the operational simplicity of node groups is valuable.
- Both require PDBs and working graceful shutdown on apps — consolidation drains nodes; apps that don't handle SIGTERM drop requests.

**Gotchas**
- PodDisruptionBudgets must be set correctly — without them consolidation and scale-down cause availability hits.
- Pod density limits per instance type (AWS VPC CNI IP limits) — small instances only run 10 pods; autoscaler bin-packing must respect this.
- Karpenter's consolidation can be aggressive — `consolidateAfter: 30s` is fine for cost optimization but moves pods frequently; raise it if churn is a problem.

questions.question: What is the Vertical Pod Autoscaler and when should you use it for JVM workloads?
questions.title: Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): Right-Sizing Pod Resource Requests
questions.direct_answer: VPA observes actual pod CPU/memory usage over time and recommends or automatically applies adjusted `requests` and `limits`. It runs in three modes: **Off** (recommendations only), **Initial** (applies at pod creation), and **Auto** (evicts and recreates pods with new resources). Use **VPA Recommender only** for JVMs — `Auto` evicts pods to resize, which causes churn; HPA + VPA on the same CPU/memory dimension fight each other. Best pattern: VPA-recommend for initial right-sizing discovery, then apply recommendations manually or via GitOps; HPA for horizontal; Karpenter for nodes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand VPA's three modes, the HPA/VPA conflict, and why Auto mode is risky for JVMs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running VPA in Auto mode alongside HPA on CPU (they fight), or expecting VPA to resize live without restart (it cannot — resize requires pod eviction + recreation)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain in-place resize KEP (alpha, no eviction), recommender algorithm (percentile-based), why VPA is best as a recommendation source for capacity planning, and the interaction with LimitRange

sections.title: The Sizing Problem VPA Addresses
sections.content:
Teams ship services with resource requests and limits that are either guesses or copy-pasted from an unrelated service. The consequences:

- **Oversized requests** — the scheduler reserves more CPU/memory than the pod needs, capacity is wasted, cloud bill inflated by 30–100%.
- **Undersized requests** — too many pods packed onto a node; when load hits, they all OOMKill or throttle simultaneously.
- **Over-provisioned limits** — memory leaks grow for days before hitting a limit; OOMKill comes at the worst time.
- **Under-provisioned limits** — pod killed under GC pressure; SRE gets paged at 3 AM.

VPA reads actual usage from the metrics server over time and produces **evidence-based recommendations**: for this workload, `requests.cpu: 250m, requests.memory: 640Mi` based on P95 over 8 days.

Three modes:

- **`Off`** (recommender only) — writes recommendations to the VPA object; no changes applied.
- **`Initial`** — applies the recommended values at pod creation (restart, rolling update).
- **`Auto`** — **evicts** pods when the recommendation diverges from current settings, so the new pod comes back with new sizing.

**The critical caveat:** standard Kubernetes resize requires pod eviction (in-place resize is still alpha via a KEP). `Auto` mode churns pods to resize them — disruptive for production JVMs that take 30–60s to warm up. For most JVM workloads the right pattern is **`Off` mode for recommendations**, apply changes via GitOps.

sections.title: VPA's Three Components and Their Interaction
sections.content:
VPA has a Recommender (observes usage, produces suggestions), an Updater (evicts pods in Auto mode), and an Admission Controller (rewrites resource specs on pod creation).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    MS[Metrics Server\nreal-time usage] --> Rec[VPA Recommender\npercentile analysis]
    Prom[Prometheus history\noptional] -.-> Rec
    Rec -->|write status| VPA[VerticalPodAutoscaler CRD\nstatus.recommendation]
    VPA -->|mode: Auto| Upd[VPA Updater\nevicts pods]
    Upd -->|evict| Pod[Existing Pod]
    Pod -.pod recreated.-> AC[VPA Admission Controller\nmutates resource requests]
    AC -->|applies recommendation| NewPod[New Pod with resized requests]
    Deploy[Deployment] --> NewPod
    HPA[HPA target same Deployment] -.conflict on CPU/memory.-x Rec
```

When a pod is recreated (by Deployment rollout, eviction, or scale event), the Admission Controller rewrites its resource spec to match the VPA recommendation — this is how `Initial` mode works. `Auto` adds the Updater's eviction loop on top.

sections.title: Deploying VPA in Recommender-Only Mode for Safe Right-Sizing
sections.content:
Install VPA components via the kubernetes/autoscaler Helm chart:

```bash
helm install vpa fairwinds/vpa -n kube-system
```

Attach a VPA to a Deployment in `Off` mode:

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: spring-app-vpa
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: spring-app
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: "Off"       # recommendations only, no auto action
  resourcePolicy:
    containerPolicies:
      - containerName: app
        minAllowed: {cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi}
        maxAllowed: {cpu: 4,    memory: 8Gi}
        controlledResources: ["cpu", "memory"]
```

After ~48 hours of observation:

```bash
kubectl describe vpa spring-app-vpa
# Recommendation:
#   Container Name:  app
#   Lower Bound:     cpu: 120m,   memory: 380Mi
#   Target:          cpu: 250m,   memory: 640Mi
#   Upper Bound:     cpu: 480m,   memory: 1024Mi
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Target** — what VPA would apply in Auto mode; the recommended `requests`.
- **Lower bound** — minimum to avoid resource starvation.
- **Upper bound** — maximum before you would over-provision.

Commit these recommendations into your Deployment manifest and let GitOps roll them out. This is **evidence-based capacity planning** without the churn of Auto mode. Repeat every few quarters as workload characteristics change.

sections.title: Why HPA and VPA Conflict on CPU/Memory (and How to Combine Them Safely)
sections.content:
**The conflict:**

- HPA watches CPU utilization (current / requests) and scales the replica count.
- VPA observes actual usage and resizes `requests`.
- If VPA doubles the request, HPA's utilization percentage halves — HPA scales down.
- If HPA scales up, more pods share load, actual per-pod usage drops — VPA recommends smaller requests.

They oscillate. **Do not run HPA and VPA in `Auto` mode on the same dimension (CPU or memory).**

**Safe combinations:**

- **HPA on custom metrics + VPA on CPU/memory (`Auto` or `Initial`)** — HPA scales on RPS / queue depth, VPA right-sizes per-pod CPU. No conflict.
- **HPA on CPU + VPA `Off` mode** — VPA only recommends, you apply manually via GitOps; no live resizing.
- **HPA on CPU + VPA on memory only** — set `controlledResources: [memory]` on VPA; HPA scales CPU-driven replicas, VPA resizes memory.

The pragmatic default for most Java shops: **HPA for horizontal scaling, VPA in `Off` mode for periodic right-sizing review, no `Auto` mode anywhere.** This captures the observability benefit of VPA without churn.

sections.title: When VPA Auto Is Fine, When It's Risky, and the In-Place Resize Future
sections.content:
**When `Auto` is fine:**

- **Stateless single-replica workloads** with short startup — admin pods, batch jobs, side tools.
- **Dev/staging clusters** for cost optimization; churn is tolerable.
- **Non-HPA Deployments** where horizontal scaling is not configured.

**When `Auto` is risky:**

- **JVM services with long warm-up** — eviction costs 30–60s of cold-start latency per affected pod; daily churn hurts P99.
- **HPA-driven workloads** — dimension conflict as above.
- **Services with warm caches** (local guava/Caffeine) — every eviction empties the cache.
- **Services with long-lived connections** (WebSockets, SSE) — eviction breaks connections.
- **PDB constraints** — VPA eviction respects PDB, but if PDB is strict, evictions block and recommendations never apply.

**In-place pod resize (KEP-1287, alpha in 1.27, beta in 1.33).** Changes resource requests on a running pod without eviction. Once GA, `Auto` mode becomes safe for long-warm-up services. Today: alpha gate, careful evaluation only.

**Interaction with LimitRange.** VPA recommendations can be clipped by namespace `LimitRange.max` — if VPA recommends 2Gi memory but LimitRange caps at 1Gi, the applied value is 1Gi. Monitor `kube_vpa_status_recommendation` vs actual pod requests for divergence.

**Interaction with Karpenter.** VPA resizing individual pods does not directly change node count. But VPA's right-sized requests lead to better bin-packing by Karpenter — fewer oversized reservations means tighter node utilization and lower cost.

**Recommender algorithm.** VPA uses a percentile-based decay model — newer samples weighted more. Target = P90 of CPU usage + buffer. Memory based on peaks. Observation window ~8 days by default; configurable via `--recommender-interval`.

**Observability signals:**

- `vpa_cpu_recommendation_target{container=...}` vs actual pod requests — divergence = apply recommendations.
- `kube_vpa_status_condition{type=NoPodsMatched}` — VPA is attached but no pods match — misconfigured targetRef.
- Alert on eviction rate when Auto mode is used.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **VPA has three modes: Off, Initial, Auto** — Off is safest (recommendations only); Auto evicts pods to resize; Initial applies on creation.
- **Current VPA resizing requires pod eviction** — in-place resize is alpha/beta (KEP-1287); Auto mode churns pods which hurts long-warm-up JVMs.
- **HPA and VPA conflict on CPU/memory** — do not run both in Auto on the same dimension; safe combos: HPA on custom metrics + VPA on CPU, or HPA on CPU + VPA Off mode.
- **Recommender-only (`Off`) mode is the pragmatic default** — use VPA as a capacity-planning tool; apply recommendations via GitOps.
- **LimitRange can clip VPA recommendations** — if `max` in LimitRange is below the recommendation, the applied value is clipped; monitor divergence.
- **Better requests → better Karpenter bin-packing** — right-sized requests improve node utilization; VPA and Karpenter compose well even without Auto mode.
- **JVMs with warm caches and long warm-up should NOT use Auto** — eviction costs cache warmth and 30–60s startup latency per event.
- **Recommender is percentile-based over ~8 days** — tune window for workloads with strong weekly seasonality.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Vertical Pod Autoscaler observes actual pod resource usage over time and produces recommendations for CPU and memory requests and limits. It has three modes with very different risk profiles.

**Three modes**
- Off — writes recommendations to the VPA object without changing anything; this is the safest mode and what most JVM shops should use.
- Initial — applies the recommended values at pod creation but does not evict running pods.
- Auto — evicts and recreates pods when the recommendation diverges from current; churns pods to resize.

**Why Off mode is usually right for JVMs**
- Current VPA resizing requires pod eviction — in-place resize is an alpha/beta feature (KEP-1287) not yet generally available.
- Evicting a Spring Boot pod costs 30 to 60 seconds of cold-start latency — daily Auto-mode resizing hurts P99.
- HPA and VPA on the same CPU/memory dimension fight each other — VPA raises requests, HPA utilization percentage drops, HPA scales down; then per-pod usage rises, VPA raises requests again.
- The pragmatic pattern: HPA for horizontal scaling, VPA in Off mode for periodic right-sizing review, apply recommendations via GitOps.

**The value VPA delivers even in Off mode**
- Evidence-based capacity planning — after 8 days of observation, VPA tells you exactly what this workload needs at P90 CPU and peak memory.
- Removes guesswork from resource requests — teams typically overprovision by 30 to 100 percent; right-sized requests translate directly to cloud bill reduction.
- Better Karpenter bin-packing — tighter requests mean tighter node utilization; VPA + Karpenter compose well even without Auto mode.

**Safe combinations with HPA**
- HPA on custom metrics (RPS, queue depth) plus VPA in Auto mode on CPU/memory — no dimension conflict.
- HPA on CPU plus VPA in Off mode only — VPA recommends, you apply via GitOps.
- HPA on CPU plus VPA controlling only memory via `controlledResources: [memory]` — HPA scales on CPU utilization, VPA right-sizes memory without interfering.

**Gotchas to watch**
- LimitRange can clip VPA recommendations — if namespace LimitRange max is below the recommendation, VPA's applied value is clipped silently.
- PDBs block Auto-mode evictions — strict PDBs mean VPA cannot resize; recommendations linger without being applied.
- Recommender window is ~8 days by default — for workloads with weekly seasonality, extend the window or stage recommendations over multiple cycles.
